title: Trinity Sunday
hook: the one Sunday for the mystery at the heart of it all

segments.voice: Yesterday, glossa: wind, fire, and a crowd hearing the news in their own languages. Your line was every tongue.

A legend is told about Augustine, the North African bishop and writer. He's walking a beach, turning over a hard question: how can God be one, and also three? He finds a child running to the sea with a shell, pouring water into a little hole in the sand. What are you doing? Putting the sea in this hole. Augustine laughs: that's impossible. And the child answers, more or less, so is fitting God into your head. The legend doesn't need to be true to land. After Easter and Pentecost, the calendar keeps one Sunday just for that question. Today, Trinity Sunday.
screen: `THE SEA IN A HOLE IN THE SAND.`

segments.voice: Start with one God. Moses says it in Deuteronomy, in the King James Bible: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD." Jesus quotes it himself when asked which commandment comes first. And yet the Gospels keep naming three together. At Jesus's baptism in Matthew, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and a voice from heaven says, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Father speaking, Son in the water, Spirit descending, in one scene. At the end of Matthew, Jesus sends his friends out "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." Some Christian readers point out: the name, not the names. And Paul signs off a letter: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." Over time the church found a word for what these texts hold together: Trinity. One God, say Christians who hold the creeds, in three persons. Not three gods. Not one God wearing three masks. Father, Son and Spirit, each fully God, and one. Some teachers say every picture falls short: shamrocks, water and ice and steam help a little, then leak. That's why Christians call it a mystery: not a puzzle awaiting a clever answer, but something held true that you can live inside without reaching the bottom. The sea doesn't fit in the hole. People still swim in it.
screen: `THE LORD OUR GOD IS ONE LORD.`
`FATHER, SON AND SPIRIT IN ONE SCENE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you know is true but can't fully explain: the way a parent loves three children completely, or what a person is, really, behind the face. If you pray, rest in Paul's farewell, the grace of Christ, the love of God, the communion of the Spirit; if you don't, let the big thing stay big, and sit beside it.
Trinity Sunday. The Sunday after Pentecost, for the Christian belief in one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit: in Christian words, a mystery, not a puzzle.
Your line: three in one. Some things are for living inside, not for solving. That's day one thousand forty-two.

howItsDone: On Trinity Sunday some churches sing hymns to the Trinity and say a creed, and preachers often take up the texts where Father, Son and Spirit are named together.

chat.says: Why call the Trinity a mystery? Is it just a puzzle nobody's solved yet?
options: A mystery here isn't a puzzle; it's held true, and you can live inside it.
Yes, it's a puzzle theologians expect to crack with a clever enough answer.
It means a secret that only clergy are allowed to have explained to them.
chat.meaning: In Christian use, a mystery isn't a puzzle waiting for an answer. It's held to be true and lived inside, like swimming in the sea.

notes: The Augustine and the child on the beach story is presented as 'a legend told about Augustine'; confirm framing.
'Teachers in the tradition say that every picture for this falls short' is a general claim; soften to 'some teachers' if a Keeper prefers.

Trinitarian summary (one God in three persons; not three gods, not one God in three masks) is attributed to 'Christians who hold the creeds'; confirm it is fair and that non-Trinitarian groups are neither named nor judged.
'Over time the church found a word' avoids any date for the term 'Trinity'.
Original left null: τριάς is a church term, not a biblical word, so no original-language word is taught.
